```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(parameters)
library(performance)
library(apa7)
library(psych)
```

```{r}
#| label: setup2
#| eval: false
<<setup>>
```


The apa7 package is closely aligned with the [easystats](https://easystats.github.io/easystats/) suite of packages for reporting statistical analyses. In most cases, it relies on easystats functions to do most of the hard work and then converts the output to APA style tables. For example, the easystats package parameters has a function `model_parameters` that takes regression fit objects and displays regression coefficient tables into a `tibble` that is displayed as a markdown table. The `apa_parameters` function converts the output of `model_parameters` into a `tibble` that is ready for `apa_flextable` to display as an APA-style table. The workflow has three steps:

1. Make a regression model fit object with `lm`, `glm`, or a similar function.
2. `apa_parameters` converts the fit object into a tibble using easystats functions.
3. `apa_flextable` converts the tibble into an APA-style table.

Because step 2 returns a tibble, you can post-process it with dplyr before step 3. In Quarto and R Markdown documents, however, the output of `apa_parameters` is displayed as an APA-style table automatically, so step 3 is only needed when you want to customize the table or save it.


# Linear Regression

```{r}
#| label: ACT

d <- sat.act |>
  mutate(
    gender = factor(
      gender,
      levels = 1:2,
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = 0:5,
      labels =     c("None", "High School", "Some College", "Bachelor", "Master", "Doctorate")
    )
  ) |>
  tidyr::drop_na()

lm1 <- lm(ACT ~ age + gender, d)
lm2 <- update(lm1, . ~ . + education)
lm3 <- update(lm2, . ~ . + SATV + SATQ)
```



In the console, `apa_parameters` prints as an ordinary tibble, so you can inspect it. Here `as_tibble` is used to show that tibble in this document.

```{r}
#| label: lm-tibble
apa_parameters(lm1) |>
  tibble::as_tibble()
```

In a rendered document, the output of `apa_parameters` is displayed as a table without further processing.

```{r}
#| label: lm-auto
apa_parameters(lm1)
```

The output is still a tibble, so ordinary dplyr verbs work. Pass the result to `apa_flextable` to customize the table. For example, to drop the intercept:

```{r}
#| label: lm-filter
apa_parameters(lm1) |>
  filter(Variable != "Constant") 
```

To compare nested models, pass a list. Model fit statistics (*R*^2^, change in *R*^2^, and the *F* test of the change) are added automatically.

```{r}
#| label: lm-list
apa_parameters(list(lm1, lm2, lm3))
```

# Binary Logistic Regression

`apa_parameters` also accepts `glm` objects. The table reports coefficients on the link scale (*B*), their standard errors, the exponentiated coefficient, and the test statistic. For logistic regression, the exponentiated coefficient is the odds ratio (*OR*), and the test statistic is *z*.

```{r}
#| label: glm1
glm1 <- glm(am ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars, family = binomial)
apa_parameters(glm1)

```

Exponentiated coefficients are added whenever the link function is logit or log. They are labeled *OR* for logit links, *IRR* (incidence rate ratio) for log links in count models, and *RR* (risk ratio) for log links in binomial models. Set `exponentiate = FALSE` to leave them out, or `exponentiate = TRUE` to add them for other links such as probit.

```{r}
#| label: glm-noexp
apa_parameters(glm1, exponentiate = FALSE)
```

To choose and order the columns, use `predictor_parameters`. Columns that the model does not report (for example, *t* for a model tested with *z*) are dropped silently.

```{r}
#| label: glm-columns
apa_parameters(
  glm1,
  predictor_parameters = c("Parameter", "Exp_Coefficient", "z", "p")
)
```

As with `lm`, `starred` and `bolded` mark significant coefficients.

```{r}
#| label: glm-starred
apa_parameters(glm1, starred = "Coefficient", bolded = "p")
```

## Comparing logistic regression models

A list of `glm` models is displayed with a pseudo-*R*^2^ (Tjur's for logistic regression, as chosen by `performance::r2`) and a likelihood ratio test of the change, because the binomial family has a fixed dispersion parameter.

```{r}
#| label: glm-list
glm0 <- glm(am ~ wt, data = mtcars, family = binomial)
apa_parameters(list(glm0, glm1))
```

The model comparison can also be displayed separately with `apa_performance_comparison`.

```{r}
#| label: glm-compare
apa_performance_comparison(list(glm0, glm1))
```

# Multinomial Logistic Regression

When the outcome has more than two unordered categories, multinomial logistic regression (`nnet::multinom`) compares each category with a reference category, which is the first level of the outcome. The `Womenlf` data set in the carData package has the work participation of 263 married Canadian women (not working, working part time, or working full time), their husbands' income (in $1,000s), and whether they had children at home. Here, not working is the reference category:

```{r}
#| label: multinom
d_work <- carData::Womenlf |>
  mutate(
    participation = factor(
      partic,
      levels = c("not.work", "parttime", "fulltime"),
      labels = c("Not working", "Part time", "Full time")
    ),
    husband_income = hincome
  )

multinom1 <- nnet::multinom(
  participation ~ husband_income + children,
  data = d_work,
  trace = FALSE
)

apa_parameters(multinom1) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

Each comparison gets a heading row with its coefficients indented below it, and the exponentiated coefficients are odds ratios relative to the reference category. Women with children at home had much lower odds of working full time than of not working, but children made little difference to the odds of working part time. To compare the categories with another reference, reorder the levels of the outcome (e.g., with `relevel`) before fitting the model. With `category_headings = FALSE`, each row is labeled with its category instead (e.g., "Part time: Constant").

Lists of multinomial models are compared with McFadden's pseudo-*R*^2^ and likelihood ratio tests:

```{r}
#| label: multinom-list
multinom0 <- nnet::multinom(participation ~ husband_income, data = d_work, trace = FALSE)
apa_performance_comparison(list(multinom0, multinom1))
```

# Count Regression

For Poisson and negative binomial regression, the exponentiated coefficients are incidence rate ratios (*IRR*).

```{r}
#| label: poisson
glm_pois <- glm(carb ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars, family = poisson)
apa_parameters(glm_pois)
```

Quasi-families and other families with an estimated dispersion parameter are tested with *t* instead of *z*, and the degrees of freedom are shown in the column header. Nested models are compared with *F* tests instead of likelihood ratio tests.

```{r}
#| label: quasipoisson
glm_qpois <- glm(carb ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars, family = quasipoisson)
apa_parameters(glm_qpois)
```

## Zero-inflated and hurdle models

Counts often have more zeros than a Poisson or negative binomial model expects. A zero-inflated model (`pscl::zeroinfl`) adds a logistic model of *excess* zeros, which come from cases that could only be zero (e.g., scientists who were not publishing at all). A hurdle model (`pscl::hurdle`) instead has a logistic model of whether the count is zero or positive, and a zero-truncated count model of the positive counts. Either way, `apa_parameters` puts each part under its own heading. Only the count model's coefficients are exponentiated (*IRR*), because the zero model's coefficients are log odds. The `bioChemists` data set in the pscl package has the number of articles 915 biochemistry graduate students published in the last 3 years of their PhD programs, which depends here on their mentors' numbers of articles (`mentor_articles`) and their number of young children (`young_children`). The zero-inflation part has only the mentor's articles:

```{r}
#| label: zeroinfl
data("bioChemists", package = "pscl")
d_articles <- bioChemists |>
  rename(
    articles = art,
    mentor_articles = ment,
    young_children = kid5
  )

zinb <- pscl::zeroinfl(
  articles ~ mentor_articles + young_children | mentor_articles,
  data = d_articles,
  dist = "negbin"
)

apa_parameters(zinb) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

Students with productive mentors published more, and they were less likely to be among those who did not publish at all. The note names the count distribution, gives the negative binomial dispersion parameter (*&theta;*), and explains the zero model. For a hurdle model, the zero model's heading is "Zero hurdle model", and its coefficients are the log odds of a count greater than zero:

```{r}
#| label: hurdle
pscl::hurdle(
  articles ~ mentor_articles + young_children | mentor_articles,
  data = d_articles,
  dist = "negbin"
) |>
  apa_parameters() |>
  apa_note()
```

`apa_performance_comparison` compares nested zero-inflated or hurdle models with likelihood ratio tests.

For nested counts, or counts with many zeros, negative binomial and zero-inflated mixed models fit with glmmTMB are described in the [multilevel article](multilevel.html#count-outcomes-with-glmmtmb).

# Collinearity

`apa_collinearity` reports the variance inflation factor (*VIF*) and tolerance of each predictor, as computed by `performance::check_collinearity`. In the third ACT model above, the two SAT scores are correlated, but not enough to inflate their standard errors much:

```{r}
#| label: collinearity
apa_collinearity(lm3) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

Education has more than 1 degree of freedom, so its *VIF* is the generalized *VIF*, and the note says so. Add `"SE_factor"` to `columns` for *VIF*^1/(2*df*)^, which can be compared across terms with different degrees of freedom. To bold large *VIF*s, set `flag` to your cutoff (e.g., `flag = 5` or `flag = 10`). In models with interactions, the *VIF*s of the interaction and its components are high in part because product terms are correlated with their components, and the note explains that this does not affect the test of the interaction.

```{r}
#| label: collinearity-interaction
lm(ACT ~ SATV * SATQ, data = d) |>
  apa_collinearity(flag = 10) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```


With centered predictors, these *VIF*s are small, and the note leaves this out.

```{r}
#| label: collinearity-interaction-centered
lm(ACT ~ SATV * SATQ, data = datawizard::center(d)) |>
  apa_collinearity(flag = 10) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

# Table Notes

A regression table often needs a note that defines its symbols and explains its stars. `apa_parameters` records how each table was made, and `apa_note` turns that record into note text. For the hierarchical regression above, the note defines the standardized coefficient and the change in *R*^2^ and explains the stars on the change in *R*^2^:

```{r}
#| label: note-lm-list
tbl_lm <- apa_parameters(list(lm1, lm2, lm3))
apa_note(tbl_lm)
```

The note changes with the table. With robust standard errors (`vcov`) and confidence intervals, it says which standard errors were used and defines CI:

```{r}
#| label: note-robust
apa_parameters(
  lm3,
  predictor_parameters = c("Parameter", "Coefficient", "SE", "CI", "t", "df_error", "p"),
  vcov = "HC3"
) |>
  apa_note()
```

For logistic regression, it defines the odds ratio. For count models, it defines the incidence rate ratio, and for ordinal models, it says that thresholds are not tested. For mixed models (`lme4`), it gives the method used to approximate the degrees of freedom of the *t* tests (Kenward–Roger by default).

```{r}
#| label: note-glm
apa_parameters(glm1, starred = "p") |>
  apa_note()
```

The text is in markdown and does not start with "*Note*." because apaquarto adds that. With [apaquarto](https://wjschne.github.io/apaquarto/), use `apa_note` in the `apa-note` chunk option with `!expr`. Chunk options are evaluated before the chunk runs, so make the table in an earlier chunk (as `tbl_lm` was made above) and display it in the chunk with the note. Write it as `apa7::apa_note`, because in documents with cached chunks, chunk options can be evaluated before `library(apa7)` takes effect:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lm-note
#| tbl-cap: Hierarchical Regression Predicting ACT Scores
#| apa-note: !expr apa7::apa_note(tbl_lm)
#| echo: fenced
tbl_lm
```

Without apaquarto (e.g., in a plain Quarto or R Markdown document, or a table saved to Word with `flextable::save_as_docx`), `apa_flextable` can put the note below the table itself. With `note = TRUE`, it uses the note from `apa_note`; a character string is used as the note instead. The note is added after the column widths are set, so a long note does not stretch the table.

```{r}
#| label: lm-flextable-note
apa_parameters(glm1, starred = "p") |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

Do not use `note` with the `apa-note` chunk option, or the note will appear twice.

The definitions come from the `abbreviation` slot of each column's format, so any column with a definition is defined in the note. Symbols such as *SE* and *t* have no definition by default. To add one, or to reword a definition, change the slot in the `column_formats` passed to `apa_parameters` (or set it for every table with `apa7_defaults(column_formats = cf)`):

```{r}
#| label: note-abbreviation
cf <- column_formats()
cf$SE@abbreviation <- "standard error"
cf$Std_Coefficient@abbreviation <- "standardized regression coefficient"
apa_parameters(lm1, column_formats = cf) |>
  apa_note()
```

The generated note is a starting point. Add to it with `paste` (e.g., `paste(apa_note(tbl_lm), "Education was dummy coded with None as the reference group.")`), or use `collapse = NULL` to get one sentence per element, so you can drop or reword sentences. `apa_note` reads an attribute of the table that dplyr functions such as `mutate` and `filter` keep but some operations (e.g., joins) drop, so call it on the table that `apa_parameters` returned.

# Printing Options

The `apa7.print` option controls how the output of `apa_parameters`, `apa_performance`, and `apa_performance_comparison` is displayed.

* `"auto"` (default): table in Quarto and R Markdown documents, tibble in the console.
* `"flextable"`: table everywhere.
* `"tibble"`: tibble everywhere.

```{r}
#| label: print-option
#| eval: false
options(apa7.print = "flextable")
```

To get the table with non-default settings, pass the output to `apa_flextable`, which always returns a flextable.
